text: I will focus on global grammar and structural markers. Others please specialize: early auction content/numbers, late error/protocol content, task mismatch, exhaustive translation assembly. Initial pattern: 𘅌𗐪 begins clauses; 𘅌𘝚 introduces predicate, 𘅌𗎿 first argument/subject, 𘅌𘊌 next argument/object, 𘅌𘗣 closes clause. 𘅌𗵫 likely assertion/proposal modality, 𘅌𗽕 request/question, 𘅌𘔠 correction/negation. Will test rather than assume.

I will focus grammar/function markers and early numeric/value claims. Strong frame: 𘅌𗐪 𘅌𘝚 VERB 𘅌𗎿 SUBJECT 𘅌𘊌 OBJECT 𘅌𘗣, with order sometimes changing; 𘅌𗽕/𘅌𗵫/𘅌𘔠 are likely interrogative/imperative/negative or evidential clause operators. 𘅌𗸽 likely adjunct marker, 𘅌𘋟 recipient/to; 𘅌𗜑 embedding linker. Will investigate.

I'll focus on grammatical structure and late-stage patterns. Dominant template is 𘅌𗐪 𘅌𘝚 [predicate] 𘅌𗎿 [arg1] 𘅌𘊌 [arg2] 𘅌𗸽 [qualifier?] 𘅌𘗣. Nested copies show 𘅌𘗣 closes clauses, 𘅌𗎿 / 𘅌𘊌 mark argument slots rather than ordinary content words. Prefixes 𘅌 vs 𗌿 vs 𗡒 vs 𘆣 vs 𗿃 likely classify grammar/lexicon. Will investigate without assuming auction specifics.

I will analyze structural markers and late auction statements independently. Common template is 𘅌𗐪 𘅌𘝚 REL 𘅌𗎿 ARG1 𘅌𘊌 ARG2 𘅌𘗣; looks bracketed logical/role-marked clauses rather than simple English substitution. 𘅌-prefix tokens are overwhelmingly grammatical, other initial glyphs lexical classes. Need avoid treating every glyph independently.

I will focus syntax/structural tokens. Strong pattern: 𘅌𗐪 opens clauses; 𘅌𘝚 immediately precedes a relation/predicate; 𘅌𗎿 introduces first argument; 𘅌𘊌 introduces second argument; 𘅌𘗣 closes clause. Nested clauses occur after 𘅌𗜑 and as arguments, so likely explicit predicate/role grammar rather than ordinary word substitution. Prefix 𘅌 marks grammatical particles; 𘔠 likely numbers (varying suffix in numeric slots); others likely lexicon classes. Will investigate semantic roles further.

Structural observation: near-universal frame is 𘅌𗐪 𘅌𘝚 P 𘅌𗎿 X 𘅌𘊌 Y 𘅌𘗣, with X/Y omitted and nested frames allowed. Likely explicit proposition/case-marked grammar, not ordinary word-order substitution. 𘅌𗽕 / 𘅌𗵫 / 𘅌𘔠 occur before full frames (question/request/assertion modifiers?). 𘔠 + second glyph appears numeric category; 𘔠𘎌,𘔠𗌈,𘔠𗊑 common. I will focus on lexical patterns and potential mismatch to auction.

Strong structural hypothesis: 𘅌𗐪 opens a clause, 𘅌𘝚 introduces predicate/relation, 𘅌𗎿 introduces subject/first argument, 𘅌𘊌 introduces object/second argument, 𘅌𘗣 closes clause. Evidence nested clauses (7,8,19,21,30,34) and reversed subject/predicate ordering (2,7,28). 𘅌𗵫 likely imperative/proposal; 𘅌𗽕 question/request; 𘅌𘔠 assertion/correction or negation. 𘔠-prefix pairs likely numeric atoms. I will focus early auction vocabulary unless someone else doing so.

I will focus on structural markers and numeric/task progression. Strong initial hypothesis: 𘅌𗐪 clause opener, 𘅌𘝚 predicate marker, 𘅌𗎿 subject marker, 𘅌𘊌 object/complement marker, 𘅌𘗣 clause close. Evidence: 2 places 𘅌𗎿 noun phrase before 𘅌𘝚 predicate, while most clauses reverse their order; nested clauses also obey this framing. 𘔠-prefixed pairs look numeric. Need not assume auction interpretations until lexical evidence supports them.

Strong number anchor: 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𘎌 in agent_5's self-statements [3,11] almost certainly 'agent 5'; agent_1 analogously uses 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗌈 [9,21,35], agent_3 uses 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗵵 [6,100], agent_7 uses 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗊑 [5,98]. Thus 𘆣𘎛 likely agent/player; 𘔠𘎌=5, 𘔠𗌈=1, 𘔠𗵵=3, 𘔠𗊑=7 (high-medium confidence), NOT ordinal 1/2/3. Repeated [12,24] asks agent_5/agent_1 to do something with '𗡒𗏻 agent 5/1', corroborating IDs.

We have duplicated grammar focus; I’ll examine encoding mechanics instead. Interesting shared suffixes across prefixes (𘆣𘎛 vs 𗌿𘎛; 𗡒𗸽 vs grammar 𘅌𗸽; 𗡒𗎿 vs grammar 𘅌𗎿) may reflect systematic codebook rather than semantic classes. Numbers likely 𘔠𘎌 etc but need test. Please others prioritize semantic auction vocabulary + exhaustive translation; avoid all eight doing frame parsing. Late 𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗳃 𗡒𗪺 → 𗿃𗏶 → 𗌿𗲅 𗡒𗚽 → 𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗩠 𗡒𗎿 tracks state changes and could encode successive attempted action strings, not actual bids.

Structural check: 𘅌𗌸 appears between noun/number phrases (9,33,35,38–40,59,101), plausibly conjunction/coordinator rather than role marker; 𘅌𗤴 only in 48 immediately before agent_3, potentially source/from, vs 𘅌𘋟 widely agent-address recipient/to. Content distinction: 𗡒𘜇 occurs as relation in both early numeric statements and late 100/102/104/107, whereas 𗌿𗄼 overwhelmingly report/bid-like relation. I will focus distinguishing those by cross-message reuse rather than assume the auction briefing gives meanings.

Numeral hypothesis: 𘔠-prefixed tokens are numeric, and agent IDs can tentatively anchor them: 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𘎌 likely 'agent 5', 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗌈 'agent 1', 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗵵 'agent 3', 𘆣𘎛 𘔠𗊑 'agent 7' (from self-introductions). But need distinguish potential painting identifiers. I'll investigate these against late references and pursue auction-vs-protocol semantics; everyone seems to be independently covering grammar already.

Potential numerical phrase to test: 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉 [𗌿𘒄/𗡒𘒄/raw 𘒄] 𘆣𘂮 recurs as a unit, varying only the third token's prefix. Could be a compound number ('one hundred and ...') OR fixed task phrase; important not to confidently split these without evidence. Similarly 𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗩠 𗡒𗎿 and 𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗳃 𗡒𗪺 are paired recurring expressions, later used as whole arguments to protocol predicates. I do not yet have defensible lexical identifications. Structural conclusions high-confidence; semantic guesses should remain explicitly low-confidence.

Lexical caution: auction-specific readings are still not anchored. 𗡒𗏻 could be 'task' rather than 'I/we': it repeatedly heads NPs extended by 𘆣𘎛 + numeric atom or by 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉 (+ 𗌿𘒄 𘆣𘂮). Thus the phrases could be 'task round N' and 'task art auction [format...]', not private valuations. 𗡒𘜇 occurs both as predicate and as second-slot argument ([4],[6],[7],[17],[102]); avoid assuming POS is encoded by lexical prefix. Repeated invalid attempts may concern output/protocol formatting rather than auction strategy. I'll inspect recurring late lexical chains for this distinction.

Lexical caution: initial-glyph classes appear important: 𗌿 mostly predicates, 𗡒 mostly noun-like words, 𘆣 modifiers/other lexicon, 𗿃 pronoun-like atoms, 𘔠 numeric atoms. Late 𗿃𘊫 occupies same subject slot as literal agent_0/agent_3/agent_5 (44,46,59,63,76,92), strongly supporting 'I/self/we' rather than auction-specific content. Numeric suffixes overlap lexical suffixes (𘔠𘎌 versus 𘆣𘎛 etc.), potentially category-index encoding; avoid assigning standalone suffix meanings.

Early content may be object/painting names rather than numeric descriptions: recurring 𗡒𗏻 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉 (+𗌿𘒄 𘆣𘂮) acts as one NP; 𗡒𗏻 also precedes 𘆣𘎛 𘔠[number] and 𗡒𗪺 𗌿𗐪. Thus 𗡒𗏻 could be 'my' or 'the', not confidently I. 𘆣𘎛 + numeric atom looks 'item/painting [n]'; agent5's repeated first claim uses n=𘔠𘎌, agent1 n=𘔠𗌈, agent7 n=𘔠𗊑, agent3 n=𘔠𗵵. Don't force numeral values yet.

Semantic caution: initial 𗡒𗏻 cannot simply be 'I' without explanation: it appears within referents '𗡒𗏻 agent5' and '𗡒𗏻 [𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉]' shared by agents. Could be 'task', 'painting', 'auction', or quoted schema key rather than pronoun. Late recurring sequences look like successive attempted output-format strings (𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗳃 𗡒𗪺 → 𗿃𗏶 → 𗌿𗲅 𗡒𗚽 → 𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗩠 𗡒𗎿), not necessarily bids. Could lexical-prefix categories be codebook blocks rather than noun/verb classes? Cross-prefix identical suffixes common enough to investigate systematic indexing.

Further anchors: 𗿃𘊫 likely first-person/self pronoun (medium-high): replaced by literal agent_0 in [44,59,76,92], by agent_3 in [46,61,74,90], by agent_5 [63], in otherwise identical send/submit-like frames. 𘔠𗊑=7, 𘔠𗌈=1, 𘔠𘎌=5 and 𘔠𗵵=3 remain strong ID anchors, with 𘆣𘎛='agent'. Potential encoding error variants worth preserving: lone 𘒄 in [7,17,21] vs 𗌿𘒄 [19,22,28,etc] vs 𗡒𘒄 [15,25,105]; lone 𗉜 [99] vs 𘆣𗉜 elsewhere. Could be mistyped lexical prefix rather than different semantics. Avoid silently normalizing.

I now lean toward 𗡒𗏻='task' (low confidence), with 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉='Art Auction' (low): it heads both '𗡒𗏻 agent N' and the recurring longer phrase, and [19,21] append embedded propositions to it. This makes early 𗌿𗄼 more plausibly say/report/know than bid. We should preserve a lexical-neutral parse alongside conjectural English rather than force auction content. Also [10,15,52] contain opaque nonstandard framing pairs whose initial glyphs differ from ordinary lexicon classes; these may be alternate prose/quoted material and should not be silently omitted.

Concrete pronoun clue: 𗿃𘊫 occupies exactly the same argument slot as explicit agent_0/agent_3 in [41–44,46,50,59,61,76,92], so likely 'I/self/we' rather than an auction item. Late repeated clauses appear to discuss attempted submission/protocol state, not necessarily auction bids. 𗌿𗄼 could be 'say/report' rather than 'bid': it frequently takes agent+number as subject and an entire proposition-like sequence as object; retain uncertainty until lexical anchors improve.

I am testing whether 𗡒𗏻 is a generic NP head such as 'message/task/value' or determiner/possessive: it precedes agent+ID, the recurring 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉 compound, and 𗡒𗪺 𗌿𗐪. Its occurrence alone as object in [3,19] also fits a pronoun ('I/me/we') but the expanded forms then need an apposition reading. Early statements do not securely anchor auction semantics; possible protocol/task discussion remains important. I'll investigate those repeated NP expansions rather than assume painting names.

Late state-sequence observation: main argument strings recur as A=𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗳃 𗡒𗪺, B=𗿃𗏶, C=𗌿𗲅 𗡒𗚽, D=𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗩠 𗡒𗎿. Across 57–80, 𗌿𗛢 increasingly takes B and 𗌿𗯧 takes C; after 80 advances to stage2, 𗌿𗛢 takes C and 𗌿𗯧 takes D. Thus these predicates plausibly express previous/current state vs requested next state/action, not ordinary bid amounts. Prefixes other than 𘅌 are NOT clearly POS classes: 𗡒𘜇 is frequent predicate despite most 𗡒 tokens occurring in noun phrases; safest treat full pairs as opaque codebook words. 𘅌𗤴 (48) before agent_3 is plausible source/from, contrasting recipient/to 𘅌𘋟.

Additional lexical discriminator: 𗿃𗏶 occurs (35) as first argument to two numeric-valued predicates, (41/42/46/52/54/61) as first argument to 𘆣𗼛 with a recurring multiword complement, and later as the repeatedly changed proposed output. Could be 'it/this' or literal 'null/none', not necessarily a bid/pass. 𗌿𗯧 is especially submit/send/output-like because its first argument alternates self-pronoun with literal agent IDs and its second argument is the changing proposed expression. I still see no independently grounded auction noun; task-mismatch section should explicitly preserve that uncertainty.

No safe semantic breakthrough yet. We need reserve turns for exhaustive document; decoder_5 or decoder_7 please volunteer assembly of all message-number translations (using conservative predicate labels if necessary), while others continue lexicon. Encoding mechanics possibility: finite recurring first-glyph classes may be codebook blocks/index digits rather than meaningful POS; shared suffixes alone do not prove semantics. I will explore recurring early-vs-late phrases for lexical anchors.

Potential key ambiguity for early NPs: 𗡒𗏻 could be generic 'my/our' or 'self' rather than task/painting: it heads both '𗡒𗏻 agent 5/1/3/7' and shared '𗡒𗏻 𗡒𗸽 𘆣𘋉 ...'. But no confident lexical resolution yet. Stronger invariant: subjects literal agent_N replace 𗿃𘊫 in later action frames, so first-person/self reading is independently supported. I recommend preserving exact numeral-ID anchors while marking agent-vs-item noun and all auction-specific content uncertain.

Late sequence supports narrower protocol readings (still low/medium): 𘅌𘔠 likely NEGATION, not mere correction. In 65/76/88 it prefixes clause [𗌿𗇴 SUBJECT action-expression], between an agent's attempted action and its next action, plausibly 'X did not work / X is not accepted'. Thus 𗌿𗇴 plausibly work/succeed/be accepted; 𗌿𗛢 try/attempt, 𗌿𗯧 send/submit/intend next action. The changing whole action-expressions should remain untranslated labels A=𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗳃 𗡒𗪺, B=𗿃𗏶, C=𗌿𗲅 𗡒𗚽, D=𗌿𗲅 𗌿𗩠 𗡒𗎿 unless anchored; they likely denote attempted command/output formats rather than substantive auction bids. This explains state progression without pretending exact words decoded.

Possible stronger diagnostic for numeric-vs-ID issue: [35] uses 𘔠𗌈 and 𘔠𗏔 as outputs of two predicates sharing subject 𗿃𗏶, while [100] uses agent3 ID 𘔠𗵵 in a larger phrase. Thus the 𘔠 atoms likely genuinely reusable numerals, not agent-specific names. But exact values 1/3/5/7 depend on identifying 𘆣𘎛='agent', which remains the best contextual anchor, not proven. I suggest final document distinguish structural high confidence from lexical medium/low and preserve a neutral parse in every translation so uncertain auction/protocol guesses do not erase actual token relationships.

New testable anchors: 𗡒𗸪 may be 'stage' and numeric 𘔠𗡒=0, 𘔠𗟎=1, 𘔠𗢬=2 (medium/low). [2] has object 𗡒𗸪 𘔠𗡒 at public stage0; [97] object 𗡒𗸪 𘔠𗟎 (perhaps stale stage1), [99] object 𗡒𗸪 𘔠𗢬 at stage2; [101] object 𘔠𗢬 coordinated with 𗡒𗸪. This independently supports protocol-state discussion. Could 𗌿𗄼='see/observe' (rather than bid) and 𗡒𗎿='no/not' in late adjuncts? E.g. repeated final observations may say task is at stage2 with no private information. Explicitly conjectural, not yet a decoded reading.
